Mini-Lesson

Christianity: Social and historical developments; works of scholars (part 2)

6 missions. Guess, learn, then check. Your place is saved.

  1. Mission 1Some feminists stayed in the Church to change it. Why did others decide they had to leave?
  2. Mission 2Christians pray "Our Father". Does that mean they believe God is male?
  3. Mission 3How did a small prayer meeting in Los Angeles become a quarter of world Christianity?
  4. Mission 4Britain is now a land of many faiths. How should Christians live with neighbours who believe differently?
  5. Mission 5How could one death, long ago, put things right between God and everyone else?
  6. Mission 6Did God take our place in court, or did Jesus simply show us how to love?
Mission 1

Mission 1: Some feminists stayed in the Church to change it. Why did others decide they had to leave?

Make a guess: Some feminists stayed in the Church to change it. Why did others decide they had to leave?

Mission 1

Reform or leave?

  • All feminist theologians agree that Christianity has been shaped by patriarchy.
  • Reformists (Ruether, McFague, Johnson): the core of Christianity is liberating; remove the sexism and stay.
  • Post-Christian feminists (Daly, Hampson): the sexism is built in; Christianity cannot be repaired, so they left.
  • Post-Christian does not mean atheist: both kept a spirituality; Hampson still believes in God.
  • The question: is patriarchy a stain on Christianity, or part of its structure?
Mission 1

Mary Daly

  • Mary Daly (1928–2010), American Catholic philosopher and theologian; taught at Boston College (a Jesuit university).
  • The Church and the Second Sex (1968): a reformist call for change.
  • Beyond God the Father (1973): now post-Christian: "if God is male, then the male is God" (see Mission 2).
  • The male symbol of God sanctions male rule in church, family and society.
  • God is not a noun but a verb: "Be-ing", the power of becoming in which women share.
  • Later: Gyn/Ecology (1978) and Pure Lust (1984).
Mission 1

Daphne Hampson

  • Daphne Hampson (b. 1944), British theologian (St Andrews); Theology and Feminism (1990); After Christianity (1996). Once active in the campaign for women priests.
  • Christianity is "irredeemably sexist" because it is a historical religion: it claims a unique revelation of God in a particular past.
  • That past was patriarchal: a male Jesus, God as Father and Son, male apostles. Christians must always look back to it, so the bias can never be removed.
  • Not moral: feminism needs full equality now. Not true: after the Enlightenment, she argues, a unique divine act in one time and place is not credible.
  • She is a post-Christian theist: she believes in God, known through human experience, but not in Christ's uniqueness.
Mission 1Read the source

"Neither male nor female"

> "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus." (Galatians 3:28, WEBBE)

  • Reformists (Ruether): this is the liberating core of the Gospel; later sexism betrays it.
  • Hampson: one verse, written by a man in a patriarchal world, cannot outweigh the structure of a religion centred on a male saviour and a Father God.

Q1 How would Ruether use this verse?

Show answer

As evidence that equality is part of Christianity's original message.

Q2 Why does Hampson think it is not enough?

Show answer

Christianity remains tied to a male past; the problem is structural, not a matter of verses.

Quick check
?Why does Hampson describe Christianity as irredeemably sexist?
Mission 1Diversity

Ruether, Daly and Hampson compared

  • Is Christianity patriarchal? All three: yes, deeply.
  • Can it be reformed? Ruether: yes, from its prophetic core. Daly and Hampson: no.
  • What about Jesus? Ruether: he empties male power. Daly: Christ-worship sanctifies maleness. Hampson: his uniqueness makes the male normative.
  • God? Ruether: God/ess, the primal Matrix (her terms). Daly: God as Verb, Be-ing. Hampson: God known in experience, beyond any tradition.
  • Where do they go? Ruether stays in the Catholic Church and helps shape the Women-Church movement. Daly and Hampson leave.
Mission 1Evaluate

Can Christianity be changed, or should it be abandoned?

  • Claim: Christianity is essentially sexist and should be abandoned.
  • For: Hampson: a historical religion is tied to a patriarchal past; Daly: Christ-worship sanctifies maleness.
  • For: Centuries of reform have left many churches still male-led.
  • Against: Ruether: the prophetic tradition and Jesus' practice contain the critique of patriarchy; Galatians 3:28.
  • Against: Real change has happened: women priests and bishops; inclusive language; female images of God (see Mission 2).
  • Against (traditional Christians): God has no sex; equal dignity with different roles is not sexism.
  • Judgement criteria: Is sexism the structure or a distortion? Is a religion defined by its origins or by how it develops? Does reform answer Hampson's point about the past?
Mission 1

Impact on believers and communities

  • Language: inclusive-language Bibles, hymns and liturgies (e.g. "humankind" for "mankind").
  • Ministry: feminist theology fed the case for ordaining women.
  • Communities: Women-Church groups and women's liturgies; feminist biblical scholarship taught in many seminaries.
  • Limits: the Catholic and Orthodox Churches keep an all-male priesthood; many Christians reject feminist theology as shaped by secular ideology.
Mission check

?Priya leaves her church after many years. She still prays and believes in God, but says: "No religion that looks back to one man, in one patriarchal age, as God's unique revelation can ever treat women as equals." Whose position is closest to Priya's?

Reformists and post-Christians agree that Christianity has been patriarchal; they disagree on whether that is a stain or the structure.

Mission 2

Mission 2: Christians pray "Our Father". Does that mean they believe God is male?

Make a guess: Christians pray "Our Father". Does that mean they believe God is male?

Mission 2

Human words for God

  • Anthropomorphic language: describing God in human terms (Father, King, Judge, "the hand of God").
  • Christians believe God is spirit (John 4:24) and beyond all creatures, so no human word fits God exactly.
  • Classical theology treats such words as analogy (Thomas Aquinas) or metaphor: true in one way, not in another.
  • Mainstream teaching: God has no sex. Catholic teaching: God "is neither man nor woman: he is God" (Catechism of the Catholic Church 239).
  • Yet Christian worship has used mostly male words: Father, King, Lord, "he".
  • The question: if the words are not literal, do they still shape how people see God, and men and women?
Mission 2

McFague: metaphors and models

  • Sallie McFague (1933–2019), American theologian; Metaphorical Theology (1982), Models of God (1987).
  • All talk of God is metaphor: a model of God both "is and is not" what it says (paraphrase).
  • Trouble comes when one metaphor is taken literally and becomes an idol: e.g. God as King.
  • The monarchical model (God as king and lord over the world): distant, controlling, and male. She argues it encourages domination and passivity, and fits badly with an age of nuclear and ecological threat.
  • So she proposes new models: God as Mother, Lover and Friend, and the world as God's body.
Mission 2

McFague: God as Mother

  • Mother as creator: God brings the world to birth, from God's own being, rather than making it as an object from outside (paraphrase).
  • Mother's love (agape in her sense): love that says "it is good that you exist" and wants all its children to live and flourish.
  • Mother as judge: justice as care for all she has borne; judgement falls on what harms the whole family, including the earth.
  • Ethic: care for others and for the planet; a mother does not dominate her children.
  • McFague does not say God is female: Mother is one partial model, used with others.
Quick check
?What is McFague's main reason for proposing the model of God as Mother?
Mission 2Evaluate

Is it valid to refer to God as Mother?

  • Claim: It is valid for Christians to refer to God as Mother.
  • For: The Bible itself uses maternal images (Isaiah 49:15, 66:13; Matthew 23:37), and Julian of Norwich did so.
  • For: If God has no sex, female words are as fitting (and as limited) as male ones.
  • For: McFague: male-only language has harmful effects; Mother expresses care for all.
  • Against: Jesus taught "Father", and the name expresses the Father–Son relation in the Trinity.
  • Against: McFague's "world as God's body" may blur God and creation (a risk of pantheism).
  • Against: "Mother" may itself fix a narrow idea of women.
  • Judgement criteria: Is God-language revealed or chosen? Does any image bring a sex into God? Which images help people to know God and treat each other justly?
Mission check

?A hymn-writer writes "God our Mother". A critic replies: "That's wrong, because calling God Father shows that God is literally male." On what point do mainstream Christian teaching and feminist theologians agree, against the critic?

Almost all sides agree God is not male; the live question is which words best speak of God, and what those words do to people.

Mission 3

Mission 3: How did a small prayer meeting in Los Angeles become a quarter of world Christianity?

Make a guess: How did a small prayer meeting in Los Angeles become a quarter of world Christianity?

Mission 3

Roots: Topeka and Azusa Street

  • 1901, Topeka, Kansas: at Charles Parham's Bible school, Agnes Ozman speaks in tongues. Parham teaches tongues as the "initial evidence" of baptism in the Spirit.
  • 1906–c. 1909, Azusa Street, Los Angeles: William J. Seymour (1870–1922), an African American preacher, leads a revival in a former stable building. Meetings for hours each day, Black and white, rich and poor, women and men together: unusual in segregated America.
  • Missionaries and a newspaper, The Apostolic Faith, spread it to Europe, Africa, Asia and Latin America within a few years.
  • Pentecostal denominations form: Church of God in Christ (Pentecostal from 1907), Assemblies of God (USA, 1914), Elim (UK, 1915).
  • Roots also in the Holiness movement and earlier revivals (e.g. Wales, 1904–05).
Mission 3Read the source

The Spirit at Pentecost

> "Tongues like fire appeared and were distributed to them, and one sat on each of them. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak." (Acts 2:3–4, WEBBE)

> "But to each one is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the profit of all." (1 Corinthians 12:7, WEBBE)

  • Paul then lists gifts: wisdom, knowledge, faith, healings, miracles, prophecy, discerning of spirits, languages (tongues) and their interpretation (1 Corinthians 12:8–10).

Q1 Why do Pentecostals take their name from Acts 2?

Show answer

They expect the same filling with the Spirit, with tongues, today.

Q2 According to 1 Corinthians 12:7, who are the gifts for?

Show answer

For the good of the whole community, not for private status.

Mission 3

Main beliefs

  • Baptism in the Holy Spirit: a powerful experience of being filled with the Spirit. Classical Pentecostals: a second experience after conversion, usually shown by speaking in tongues (glossolalia).
  • Gifts of the Spirit (charismata, hence "charismatic") are for today: tongues, prophecy, healing, words of knowledge.
  • The "Fourfold Gospel": Jesus as Saviour, Baptiser in the Spirit, Healer and Coming King.
  • The Bible as the authority; personal conversion; evangelism.
  • Worship: lively, participatory, expectant: raised hands, spontaneous prayer, testimony, healing prayer.
  • Not all Pentecostals agree that tongues are the necessary evidence; many charismatics do not.
Mission 3

The Charismatic Movement after 1960

  • Charismatic = Pentecostal-style experience inside the historic churches, without leaving them.
  • 1960: Dennis Bennett, an Episcopal priest in Van Nuys, California, tells his congregation he has spoken in tongues; the news spreads nationally.
  • 1964 (UK): Anglican Michael Harper founds the Fountain Trust to support renewal across denominations.
  • 1967: the Duquesne Weekend (Pittsburgh) begins the Catholic Charismatic Renewal.
  • 1980s–90s: John Wimber's Vineyard churches ("signs and wonders"); the "Toronto Blessing" (1994); the Alpha course (Holy Trinity Brompton, London) with its Holy Spirit weekend.
  • Charismatics in sacramental churches often see Spirit baptism as a release of grace already given in baptism and confirmation, not a second blessing.
Quick check
?What best distinguishes the Charismatic Movement from classical Pentecostalism?
Mission 3

Global growth

  • Evangelicalism: defined by historian David Bebbington (Evangelicalism in Modern Britain, 1989) by four marks: Bible authority, the cross, conversion, activism. Global networks such as the Lausanne Movement (1974).
  • Pentecostal and Charismatic Christians: about 584 million in 2010, over a quarter of all Christians (Pew Research Center, 2011).
  • US: Assemblies of God and Church of God in Christ; televangelism and megachurches; strong growth among Hispanic Americans.
  • Beyond: Latin America (e.g. Brazil's Assemblies of God), Africa (e.g. Nigeria, Ghana), Asia (e.g. Yoido Full Gospel Church, Seoul). Most Pentecostals now live in the Global South.
  • Why it spreads: direct experience, healing, lay leadership, local languages and music, help for people moving to cities.
Mission 3

Migration and the African Christian diaspora

  • 1950s–60s: Caribbean migrants to Britain (the Windrush generation), often unwelcome in established churches, found churches such as the New Testament Church of God (UK, 1953).
  • From the 1980s: West African migrants plant churches: e.g. the Redeemed Christian Church of God (founded in Nigeria, 1952) and Kingsway International Christian Centre (London, 1992).
  • Black-majority churches are now a large part of churchgoing in London and other cities.
  • "Reverse mission": churches from the Global South send pastors to evangelise Europe and North America.
  • Worship travels: music, all-night prayer, fasting, expectation of healing, and languages from home.
  • Your spec: "migration as a factor in the spread of a variety of forms of Christian worship, notably in the African Christian diaspora".
Mission 3

Impact on believers and communities

  • Believers: a sense of God's closeness, assurance, healing, freedom from addiction; a new moral discipline.
  • Lay empowerment: anyone can receive gifts and minister; in many churches women preach and lead (e.g. Aimee Semple McPherson, 1920s), though others restrict leadership.
  • Communities: support for migrants (jobs, housing, language, belonging); growth where other churches decline; renewal in historic churches (e.g. Alpha).
  • Tensions: congregations split over tongues in the 1960s–70s; authoritarian leaders in some churches.
  • Prosperity gospel: some teach that faith brings health and wealth; many Pentecostals and other Christians criticise this as unbiblical.
  • Cessationists (e.g. B. B. Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles, 1918) argue that miraculous gifts ended with the apostles (cf. 1 Corinthians 13:8).
Quick check
?Which factor has most helped Pentecostal churches spread among migrants in European cities?
Mission 3

Challenge 2: natural explanation

  • Linguistics: William Samarin, Tongues of Men and Angels (1972): glossolalia sounds like language but lacks consistent grammar and meaning; it can be learned.
  • Psychology: expectation, group suggestion and music can produce falling, laughter or ecstatic speech (critics' reading of the "Toronto Blessing").
  • Neuroscience: brain scans during tongues show changed activity (e.g. reduced activity in frontal lobes: Newberg et al., 2006).
  • Response 1: a natural mechanism does not rule out a divine cause; God may work through brain and body (compare contingency miracles).
  • Response 2: judge by fruits. William James: "By their fruits ye shall know them, not by their roots" (The Varieties of Religious Experience, 1902, Lecture I).
  • Response 3: many Pentecostals accept that tongues are often not a known human language; Paul says the speaker "speaks not to men, but to God" (1 Corinthians 14:2, WEBBE).
Mission 3Evaluate

Does a natural explanation take away the religious value?

  • Claim: If charismatic experiences have a natural explanation, they have no religious value.
  • For: if the same effects come from suggestion or learning, God is not needed to explain them (Occam's razor).
  • For: unverifiable claims (ones no one else can check) cannot ground authority, especially when leaders use them to control others.
  • Against: natural process and divine action need not compete; value may lie in transformed lives (James' fruits).
  • Against: Richard Swinburne's principle of credulity (trust how things seem unless there is a special reason not to): millions report such experiences; the burden is on the sceptic.
  • Strengths and weaknesses of the movement: renewal, growth, lay participation, care for migrants vs division, emotionalism, prosperity teaching.
  • Judgement criteria: Does explaining how answer whether God is involved? What counts as evidence of the Spirit? How should fruits be measured?
Quick check
?A researcher shows that people who speak in tongues can learn the skill and that it lacks the grammar of a human language. Which reply would a Pentecostal most likely make?
Mission check

?A Catholic parish in Ireland starts a weekly prayer group where people pray for healing and some speak in tongues. The parish still celebrates Mass, and the members stay Catholic. How is this group best described?

The same experiences of the Spirit can lead people out into new churches (Pentecostal) or renew the churches they already belong to (Charismatic).

Mission 4

Mission 4: Britain is now a land of many faiths. How should Christians live with neighbours who believe differently?

Make a guess: Britain is now a land of many faiths. How should Christians live with neighbours who believe differently?

Mission 4

How Britain became multi-faith

  • 1948 on: Caribbean migrants (the Windrush generation), mostly Christian.
  • 1950s–70s: migrants from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh bring Islam, Sikhism and Hinduism to British cities.
  • 1968–72: East African Asians arrive from Kenya and Uganda.
  • 1980s on: growing migration from West Africa (Nigeria, Ghana); later from the EU (2004: e.g. Polish Catholics) and as refugees.
  • 2021 Census (England and Wales): Christian 46.2%; no religion 37.2%; Muslim 6.5%; Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist and Jewish communities each 2% or less.
  • Migration has made Britain more religiously diverse and brought many Christians: much church growth in London is in migrant-led churches.
Mission 4

Freedom of religion in a secular state

  • European Convention on Human Rights (1950), Article 9: freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including freedom to change religion and to manifest it "in worship, teaching, practice and observance".
  • Holding a belief is protected absolutely; manifesting it may be limited, but only where limits are lawful and "necessary in a democratic society" (e.g. public safety, others' rights), and no wider than needed (proportionate).
  • In UK law through the Human Rights Act 1998; the Equality Act 2010 makes "religion or belief" a protected characteristic.
  • Secular state: the state does not take sides between religions. Religious pluralism, many faiths with equal rights, is a feature of such states.
  • Britain is a mixed case: an established Church of England, with bishops in the House of Lords, in a pluralist society.
Mission 4

When Christians migrate

  • Many Windrush-era Christians, Anglicans, Methodists and Baptists at home, found a cool welcome in some English churches; many founded their own (e.g. the New Testament Church of God, in Britain from 1953).
  • Assimilation: join existing British churches, or keep a distinct identity?
  • Provision of worship: new congregations rent school halls, buy warehouses or former cinemas; planning permission and noise can be issues.
  • Style of worship: often lively, Pentecostal or Charismatic; long services; prayer and preaching in the home language.
  • Culture: second and third generations may prefer English-language worship; tension between keeping heritage and reaching British neighbours.
  • Other migrant churches: Polish Catholic parishes; Romanian and Eritrean Orthodox communities; Chinese and Korean churches.
Mission 4

Evangelical and Pentecostal growth

  • Evangelicals stress conversion, the Bible, the cross and active mission (David Bebbington's four marks, 1989).
  • Pentecostalism: from the Azusa Street revival, Los Angeles, 1906 (led by William J. Seymour); baptism in the Holy Spirit, speaking in tongues, healing, as in Acts 2.
  • Charismatic renewal (from the 1960s): the same gifts in Catholic, Anglican and other mainline churches.
  • Rapid growth in Africa, Latin America and Asia: the centre of gravity of Christianity has moved to the global South.
  • Your spec: its nature and influence "in the US and beyond", with migration spreading new forms of worship.
Mission 4

The African diaspora and reverse mission

  • African-led churches in Britain include the Redeemed Christian Church of God (founded in Nigeria, 1952), Kingsway International Christian Centre (London, 1992) and Aladura churches (e.g. Cherubim and Seraphim).
  • Features: strong prayer life, healing, prosperity teaching in some, community support for new migrants.
  • Reverse mission: Christians from countries once evangelised by Britain now send missionaries to Britain, which they see as needing re-evangelising after secularisation.
  • E.g. the RCCG aims to plant churches within a few minutes' walk of people in every country.
  • Questions: most members are migrants; reaching white British neighbours is harder. Supporters reply that growth is real and that the second generation is bridging the gap.
Quick check
?What does "reverse mission" mean?
Mission 4Evaluate

Should Christians try to convert people of other faiths?

  • Claim: Christians in a multi-faith society should seek to convert people of other faiths.
  • For: The Great Commission: "make disciples of all nations" (Matthew 28:19); exclusivist reading of John 14:6.
  • For: Reverse mission shows the energy of churches that still see evangelism as central.
  • Against: Pluralists: other faiths are valid paths; conversion is unnecessary and may harm community relations.
  • Against: Pressure to convert can damage trust between communities; community support and service to neighbours may witness better.
  • Judgement criteria: What do Christians believe about salvation? Can mission be respectful? Does it serve social cohesion? Does freedom of religion include the freedom to persuade?
  • Most UK churches, migrant-led ones included, combine witness with dialogue and practical co-operation with neighbours of other faiths.
Mission check

?A town council plans to ban door-to-door visits by all religious groups, because some residents feel pressured. Under Article 9 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which principle is at stake?

Freedom of religion covers sharing faith as well as holding it. Living with neighbours means balancing that freedom with theirs.

Mission 5

Mission 5: How could one death, long ago, put things right between God and everyone else?

Make a guess: How could one death, long ago, put things right between God and everyone else?

Mission 5

Two key terms

  • Atonement: the reconciling of God and humanity. The English word, popularised by William Tyndale's New Testament (1526, Romans 5:11), means "at-one-ment": making one again.
  • Soteriology: the study of salvation (Greek sōtēria, salvation + logos, study). What are we saved from, to, and how?
  • The problem: sin separates humans from God (Isaiah 59:2). Christians believe God offers forgiveness through Jesus' death and resurrection.
  • The creeds say Christ died "for us" but give no single theory of how this works. Several models grew up.
Mission 5Read the source

New Testament images

> "For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many." (Mark 10:45, WEBBE)

> "whom God sent to be an atoning sacrifice through faith in his blood" (Romans 3:25, WEBBE)

> "Having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it." (Colossians 2:15, WEBBE)

> "Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps" (1 Peter 2:21, WEBBE)

Q1 Match each verse to an image: ransom, sacrifice, victory, example.

Show answer

Mark 10:45 ransom; Romans 3:25 sacrifice; Colossians 2:15 victory; 1 Peter 2:21 example.

Q2 What does this suggest about later theories?

Show answer

Each develops an image already in the New Testament.

Mission 5

Sacrifice

  • Background: the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). Sin is confessed over a goat sent into the wilderness; blood is offered for cleansing.
  • "It is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life." (Leviticus 17:11)
  • Hebrews presents Jesus as both priest and offering, "once for all" (Hebrews 10:10).
  • John the Baptist: "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!" (John 1:29).
  • Sacrifice language means: a life given to restore the relationship that sin broke.
  • Aquinas lists sacrifice with merit, satisfaction and redemption as ways Christ's passion saves (Summa Theologiae III, q. 48).
  • Catholic and Orthodox Christians link this to the Eucharist, which makes present the one sacrifice of Christ.
Mission 5

Christus Victor: victory

  • Gustaf Aulén (1879–1977), Swedish Lutheran bishop: Christus Victor (lectures 1930; English 1931).
  • He called this the "classic" view: held by the early Church Fathers and, he argued, by Luther.
  • Humanity is held captive by hostile powers: sin, death and the devil. On the cross God, in Christ, fights and defeats them.
  • "through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil" (Hebrews 2:14).
  • Early ransom forms: Origen said the ransom was paid to the devil; Gregory of Nyssa pictured Christ's humanity as bait hiding the "hook" of his divinity.
  • The resurrection is the victory. The Orthodox Easter hymn: Christ is risen, "trampling down death by death".
  • Aulén: atonement is God's own act from start to finish, not humanity's offering to God.
Quick check
?Which statement best describes Aulén's "classic" view of the atonement?
Mission 5

Anselm: satisfaction

  • Anselm of Canterbury (c. 1033–1109), Cur Deus Homo ("Why God Became Man", 1098).
  • He rejected the idea that the devil had any rights over humanity to be bought off.
  • Sin robs God of the honour owed by every creature. "Every wish of a rational creature should be subject to the will of God." (I.11, trans. Deane)
  • Repaying what was taken is "the satisfaction which every sinner owes to God" (I.11).
  • God cannot just overlook this; but humans cannot pay, since they already owe God everything.
  • Only God can pay; only a human ought to. So "it is necessary for the God-man to make it" (II.6).
  • Christ's free, sinless death gives God more honour than sin took away. This is the substitution in which only the divine-human Jesus could act.
Mission 5

Substitution: Christ in our place

  • Penal substitution: Christ bears the punishment for sin in place of sinners. Developed by the Reformers (Calvin, Institutes II.16) and central to many evangelicals.
  • "He was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities." (Isaiah 53:5)
  • "For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf" (2 Corinthians 5:21); Christ became "a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13).
  • Difference from Anselm: Anselm's satisfaction is an alternative to punishment (honour restored); penal substitution is punishment, borne by another.
  • Substitution and sacrifice overlap: the sacrifice dies in the place of the sinner.
Mission 5

Moral example

  • Peter Abelard (1079–1142), Commentary on Romans (c. 1133–37).
  • The cross does not change God (who already loves); it changes us. Christ's love, shown to the death, kindles love in us and frees us from fear (paraphrase).
  • "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends." (John 15:13)
  • Jesus is the moral exemplar: how to live, and how to die, faithful and forgiving (Luke 23:34).
  • Aulén called this the "subjective" type: the change happens in the human heart.
  • Developed in liberal theology (e.g. Hastings Rashdall, The Idea of Atonement in Christian Theology, 1919) and by John Hick (see Mission 6).
Quick check
?Why did Anselm think the one who makes satisfaction must be both God and human?
Mission 5

Wrath, love and forgiveness

  • Assumption 1: humans need divine forgiveness; sin is real and serious (Romans 3:23).
  • Assumption 2: God is just. "The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness" (Romans 1:18).
  • Assumption 3: God is love. "God commends his own love towards us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (Romans 5:8)
  • How do wrath and love fit? Substitution: love provides what justice requires (1 John 4:10). Victory: wrath falls on the powers, love frees the captives. Example: God's love needs no payment, only our response.
  • Critique: if the Father punishes the Son, is God cruel? Some feminist theologians called this a picture of "divine child abuse"; Steve Chalke and Alan Mann wrote "cosmic child abuse" (The Lost Message of Jesus, 2003).
  • Replies: the Trinity acts together: "God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself" (2 Corinthians 5:19). The Son gives himself freely (John 10:18). "Wrath" is God's settled opposition to evil, not a temper.
Mission 5Diversity

Who stresses which model?

  • Eastern Orthodox: Christus Victor and theosis (sharing God's life); sin as sickness and death more than legal guilt.
  • Catholic: satisfaction and sacrifice (Anselm, Aquinas); the Mass as the sacrifice made present.
  • Reformed and evangelical: penal substitution as the heart of the gospel (with victory and example as results).
  • Liberal Protestant: moral example; doubts about punishment language.
  • Many theologians today combine them: the cross as sacrifice for sin, victory over evil, and example of love.
Mission 5Evaluate

Are the theories contradictory?

  • Claim: The theories of the atonement contradict each other.
  • For: God changes (satisfaction, substitution) versus only we change (moral example).
  • For: Anselm rejected any payment to the devil; the ransom form of Christus Victor needs one.
  • For: Satisfaction instead of punishment (Anselm) versus punishment itself (penal substitution).
  • Against: Each develops a New Testament image; Paul uses several side by side (Romans 3:25; 5:8; Colossians 2:15).
  • Against: They answer different questions: what is removed (guilt), defeated (evil), awakened (love).
  • Judge it by: Are they models (pictures) or literal mechanisms? Does each fit God as both just and loving? Does any make God cruel?
Quick check
?A critic says: "If God demands a death before he will forgive, God is cruel." Which reply comes from inside the Christus Victor tradition?
Mission check

?A hospice chaplain tells a dying man who fears death: "On the cross and in the resurrection, death itself was beaten; it no longer has the last word." Which model is she mainly using?

The same cross, several pictures: sacrifice, victory, satisfaction, substitution, example. Christians choose which to stress, often depending on the need in front of them.

Mission 6

Mission 6: Did God take our place in court, or did Jesus simply show us how to love?

Make a guess: Did God take our place in court, or did Jesus simply show us how to love?

Mission 6

Karl Barth and his context

  • Karl Barth (1886–1968), Swiss Reformed theologian; the most influential Protestant theologian of the 20th century.
  • The Epistle to the Romans (1919; rewritten 1922): God is "wholly other"; we cannot reach God, God must come to us.
  • Main author of the Barmen Declaration (1934): the Confessing Church's rejection of Nazi control of the Church. Dismissed from his post at Bonn, 1935.
  • Church Dogmatics (1932–1967, unfinished). Your extract: Volume IV, Part 1 (1953), The Doctrine of Reconciliation, §59.2, "The Judge Judged in Our Place".
  • Reformed roots: Calvin's stress on God's sovereign grace, Christ the Mediator, and the Bible as the place God speaks.
  • Anthology rule: paraphrase the extract and cite it (Extract 3).
Mission 6

"The Judge judged in our place"

  • Barth's starting point (paraphrase): sin is humanity wanting to be its own judge, to decide good and evil for itself (Genesis 3:5).
  • In Jesus Christ, God, the true Judge, comes into the world.
  • Barth explains Christ's being "for us" in four steps (paraphrase of the extract):
  • 1. He took our place as Judge: he takes back the role we tried to seize.
  • 2. He took the place of us, the accused: he stands where sinners stand.
  • 3. He was judged in our place: he suffered, was crucified and died; sin and the old sinful humanity are brought to an end in him.
  • 4. He acted justly in our place: he did the right that we failed to do, perfect obedience to God.
  • So the Judge is the judged: it is God himself, in the Son, who bears the judgement, not a third party.
Mission 6Read the source

Barth's biblical background

> "For the Father judges no one, but he has given all judgement to the Son" (John 5:22, WEBBE)

> "Now is the judgement of this world." (John 12:31, WEBBE)

> "For him who knew no sin he made to be sin on our behalf, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God." (2 Corinthians 5:21, WEBBE)

> "one died for all, therefore all died." (2 Corinthians 5:14, WEBBE)

Q1 Which verse makes the Son the Judge?

Show answer

John 5:22.

Q2 How does 2 Corinthians 5:14 support Barth's idea that sinful humanity "ends" on the cross?

Show answer

If one died for all, all died in him: the old humanity is judged and finished.

Mission 6

Guilt, judgement and forgiveness

  • Barth uses traditional forensic (courtroom) imagery: guilt, judgement, sentence, acquittal.
  • But he warns against making "punishment" the controlling idea, as if God needed to be paid off (paraphrase). The point is that sin is done away with.
  • Judgement is God's "No" to sin; it serves God's "Yes" to humanity. Forgiveness is not God overlooking sin, but God dealing with it himself.
  • Barth's doctrine of election (Church Dogmatics II/2, 1942): Jesus Christ is both the electing God and the elected human; he bears the rejection.
  • This led critics to ask whether Barth implies universalism (all will be saved). Barth refused either to affirm or to deny it.
Quick check
?In Barth's phrase "the Judge judged in our place", who is the Judge?
Mission 6

John Hick and his context

  • John Hick (1922–2012), philosopher of religion; worked in multi-faith Birmingham, later at Claremont, California.
  • Edited The Myth of God Incarnate (1977); An Interpretation of Religion (1989): religious pluralism.
  • Your extract: The Metaphor of God Incarnate (1993; 2nd edition 2005), ch. 11, "Atonement by the Blood of Jesus" (Extract 4, paraphrase only).
  • His questions: what can Christians honestly believe in a modern, scientific, multi-faith world, after the atrocities of the 20th century?
  • His Evil and the God of Love (1966): humans are created immature and grow towards goodness (an Irenaean view), rather than fallen from perfection.
Mission 6

Incarnation and resurrection as metaphor

  • Hick (paraphrase): "Son of God" was a metaphor in Jesus' world: Israel's kings were called God's sons. Later it was taken literally.
  • The Chalcedonian formula (one person, two natures) has never been given a coherent literal meaning, he argues.
  • Hick's alternative: Jesus was a man intensely open to God, through whom God's love was incarnated (embodied) to an outstanding degree. All humans can embody God's love to some degree.
  • Resurrection (Hick): the disciples' experiences after his death may have been visions (like Paul's, Acts 9); the story expresses real meaning without a physically raised body.
  • Implications (Hick): if Jesus is not literally God, the Trinity is better read as three ways the one God is experienced, not three persons.
Mission 6

Hick on atonement

  • Hick reviews the ransom, satisfaction (Anselm) and penal substitution theories, and rejects them (paraphrase of Extract 4).
  • Satisfaction reflects medieval feudal ideas of honour; penal substitution makes God's forgiveness depend on punishing an innocent.
  • Hick argues that Jesus himself taught that God forgives the repentant freely. Illustrations: the Lord's Prayer asks forgiveness directly (Matthew 6:12); in the Parable of the Lost Son the father runs to the returning son, with no payment required (Luke 15:20).
  • Sin: self-centredness, not inherited guilt. The 20th century's atrocities show its depth; what is needed is transformation, not a legal transaction.
  • Jesus is the moral exemplar: his self-giving life and death inspire us to turn from self to God (Hick's "Reality").
  • Salvation is the gradual change from self-centredness to God-centredness, found in all the great traditions.
Quick check
?Hick argues that Jesus taught free forgiveness. How does the Parable of the Lost Son illustrate his point?
Mission 6Diversity

Barth and Hick side by side

  • Who is Jesus? Barth: God the Son incarnate, fully God and fully human. Hick: a human being in whom God's love was embodied to a high degree.
  • What is sin? Barth: rebellion, wanting to be our own judge. Hick: self-centredness in immature, developing humans.
  • What does the cross do? Barth: objectively ends sin and sinful humanity; God himself bears the judgement. Hick: shows self-giving love and inspires change; nothing changes in God.
  • Resurrection: Barth: a real act of God in history, the Father's verdict on the Son. Hick: metaphor, rooted in the disciples' experiences.
  • Other religions: Barth: God is known only in his self-revelation in Christ. Hick: many religions are valid responses to the one Real.
Mission 6Evaluate

Strengths and weaknesses

  • Barth, strengths: deeply rooted in scripture and the Reformed tradition; takes sin and grace seriously; God bears the judgement himself, which defenders say answers the charge that God is cruel.
  • Barth, weaknesses: courtroom language can seem remote today; "all died in him" leaves the place of faith and the question of universalism unclear; little common ground with other faiths.
  • Hick, strengths: morally clear (no innocent punished); fits Jesus' own teaching on forgiveness; opens the way to interfaith dialogue.
  • Hick, weaknesses: departs from the creeds (Nicaea, Chalcedon); a merely exemplary death changes nothing objectively; if Jesus is one example among many, why the cross? Critics include Gavin D'Costa and Alister McGrath.
  • Judge it by: fidelity to scripture and tradition · moral coherence · power to transform lives · credibility in a pluralist age.
Mission 6

Significance today

  • Barth: shaped Reformed and evangelical theology after 1945 and influenced Catholic theologians (e.g. Hans Urs von Balthasar, Hans Küng); his stress on grace for all influences preaching of assurance and reconciliation; Barmen still inspires resistance to state control of churches.
  • Hick: shaped liberal Protestant thought, multi-faith chaplaincy and the theology of religions debate.
  • Many churches keep substitution in worship and hymns while using example for ethics: both strands remain live.
  • The question for Christians today: is the cross something God did (Barth) or something God showed (Hick)?
Quick check
?Which criticism is aimed most directly at Hick rather than at Barth?
Mission check

?After a terrorist attack, two church leaders speak. One says: "In Christ, God has already carried humanity's guilt and said his final 'No' to evil." The other says: "Jesus shows us a love strong enough to turn us from hatred; follow him, as people of every faith can." Which pairing is accurate?

Barth: the cross is God's own act of judgement and grace. Hick: the cross is an example of love that transforms. Both answer the same question about sin very differently.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • Daly: worshipping Christ sanctifies maleness, so she left Christianity.
  • Daly (Beyond God the Father, 1973): if God is male, the male is God; God as Be-ing.
  • Hampson (Theology and Feminism, 1990): Christianity is irredeemably sexist because it is tied to a unique, patriarchal past; she remains a theist.
  • Ruether reforms from within; Daly and Hampson leave.

Mission 2

  • Words like Father and King are anthropomorphic: analogies or metaphors. Mainstream Christian teaching holds that God has no sex.
  • McFague (Models of God, 1987): God as Mother, Lover, Friend; the world as God's body.

Mission 3

  • Pentecostalism: Topeka (1901) and Azusa Street (1906, Seymour); Spirit baptism, tongues, healing, the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12.
  • Charismatic Movement (from 1960): renewal within historic churches (Bennett, Fountain Trust, Catholic Renewal 1967).
  • Global growth of Evangelicalism and Pentecostalism; migration and the African Christian diaspora.

Mission 4

  • Migration since 1948 has made Britain multi-faith and brought new Christian communities; Article 9 protects belief and, within limits, its expression.
  • Migrant churches face challenges of assimilation, buildings, worship style and culture; African-led and Pentecostal churches have grown, and some see their work as reverse mission.

Mission 5

  • Atonement = reconciliation of God and humanity; soteriology = the study of salvation.
  • Models: sacrifice; victory (Aulén, Christus Victor); satisfaction and substitution (Anselm; penal substitution); moral example (Abelard).
  • The theories rest on assumptions about sin, forgiveness, and God's wrath and love; many Christians combine them.

Mission 6

  • Barth (Church Dogmatics IV/1, 1953): God the Son, the Judge, takes our place, is judged, and acts justly for us; forensic imagery serves grace.
  • Hick (The Metaphor of God Incarnate, ch. 11): incarnation and resurrection as metaphor; payment theories rejected; Jesus as moral exemplar; salvation as transformation found across religions.
  • Strengths and weaknesses turn on scripture and creed, moral coherence, objectivity, and pluralism.
